claim: Cryo-EM has revealed the structures of many challenging yet exciting macromolecular assemblies at near-atomic resolution (3–4.5Å).
source: Cryo-EM has revealed the structures of many challenging yet exciting macromolecular assemblies at near-atomic resolution (3–4.5Å), providing biological phenomena with molecular descriptions.
evidence: This is a general statement about the capabilities of cryo-EM that is supported by the broader scientific literature and the specific examples discussed in the manuscript.

claim: At near-atomic resolutions (3-4.5Å), accurately positioning individual atoms remains challenging and error-prone.
source: However, at these resolutions, accurately positioning individual atoms remains challenging and error-prone.
evidence: This claim is supported by the discussion of challenges in model building and references to prior work on model building errors.

claim: Manually refining thousands of amino acids typical in a macromolecular assembly is tedious and time-consuming.
source: Manually refining thousands of amino acids – typical in a macromolecular assembly – is tedious and time-consuming.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical challenges of manual refinement, supported by common knowledge in the field.

claim: The presented automated method can improve the atomic details in models that are manually built in near-atomic-resolution cryo-EM maps.
source: We present an automated method that can improve the atomic details in models that are manually built in near-atomic-resolution cryo-EM maps.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by the experimental results presented for three test systems.

claim: The method can improve model geometry while maintaining the fit-to-density when applied to three systems recently solved by cryo-EM.
source: Applying the method to three systems recently solved by cryo-EM, we are able to improve model geometry while maintaining the fit-to-density.
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative results presented in Tables 1 and 2 and the figures showing model quality metrics.

claim: Backbone placement errors are automatically detected and corrected by the method.
source: Backbone placement errors are automatically detected and corrected, and the refinement shows a large radius of convergence.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the examples shown in the figures, particularly for TRPV1 and mitoribosome.

claim: The refinement shows a large radius of convergence.
source: Backbone placement errors are automatically detected and corrected, and the refinement shows a large radius of convergence.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the ability to correct significant backbone errors, as shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The method is amenable to structures with symmetry.
source: The results demonstrate that the method is amenable to structures with symmetry, of very large size, and containing RNA as well as covalently bound ligands.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the successful refinement of TRPV1 (C4 symmetry) and Frh (tetrahedral symmetry).

claim: The method is amenable to structures of very large size.
source: The results demonstrate that the method is amenable to structures with symmetry, of very large size, and containing RNA as well as covalently bound ligands.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the successful refinement of the mitoribosome with 7469 amino acids.

claim: The method is amenable to structures containing RNA as well as covalently bound ligands.
source: The results demonstrate that the method is amenable to structures with symmetry, of very large size, and containing RNA as well as covalently bound ligands.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the refinement of mitoribosome (containing RNA) and Frh (containing covalently bound ligands).

claim: Advances in direct electron detectors have led cryo-EM to achieve near-atomic resolution (3–4.5 Å) using single-particle analysis.
source: Advances in direct electron detectors, as well as better image analysis algorithms, have led cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to achieve near-atomic resolution (3–4.5 Å) using single-particle analysis (Li et al., 2013; Bai et al., 2013; Scheres, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Better image analysis algorithms have led cryo-EM to achieve near-atomic resolution (3–4.5 Å) using single-particle analysis.
source: Advances in direct electron detectors, as well as better image analysis algorithms, have led cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) to achieve near-atomic resolution (3–4.5 Å) using single-particle analysis (Li et al., 2013; Bai et al., 2013; Scheres, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: At 3-4.5Å resolution, individual β-strands are resolvable in cryo-EM reconstructions.
source: Cryo-EM reconstructions at these resolutions, at which individual β-strands are resolvable and bulky sidechains are somewhat visible, make it possible to build an all-atom model directly from such maps (Kudryashev et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of cryo-EM maps at this resolution range, supported by citations.

claim: At 3-4.5Å resolution, bulky sidechains are somewhat visible in cryo-EM reconstructions.
source: Cryo-EM reconstructions at these resolutions, at which individual β-strands are resolvable and bulky sidechains are somewhat visible, make it possible to build an all-atom model directly from such maps (Kudryashev et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of cryo-EM maps at this resolution range, supported by citations.

claim: It is possible to build an all-atom model directly from cryo-EM maps at 3-4.5Å resolution.
source: Cryo-EM reconstructions at these resolutions, at which individual β-strands are resolvable and bulky sidechains are somewhat visible, make it possible to build an all-atom model directly from such maps (Kudryashev et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work demonstrating this capability.

claim: Density maps at 3-4.5Å resolution do not grant enough information to assign coordinates for each atom in the structure precisely.
source: Although sequence can be registered, density maps at this range of resolution do not grant enough information to assign coordinates for each atom in the structure precisely, and thus they cannot always capture molecular interactions for a biochemical process.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of cryo-EM at this resolution, based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Model building and refinement at near-atomic resolution is challenging and error prone.
source: Furthermore, such model building and refinement is challenging and error prone (DeLaBarre and Brunger, 2006; Brunger et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work documenting these challenges.

claim: Model-building into a cryo-EM map at near-atomic resolution generally involves manually building a model into the map with the assistance of a graphical user interface tool.
source: Model-building into a cryo-EM map at near-atomic resolution generally involves manually building a model into the map with the assistance of a graphical user interface tool (Emsley et al., 2010), followed by refinement with software repurposed from X-ray crystallography (Brown et al., 2015; Afonine et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the standard workflow in the field, supported by citations to relevant software.

claim: Model-building at near-atomic resolution is followed by refinement with software repurposed from X-ray crystallography.
source: Model-building into a cryo-EM map at near-atomic resolution generally involves manually building a model into the map with the assistance of a graphical user interface tool (Emsley et al., 2010), followed by refinement with software repurposed from X-ray crystallography (Brown et al., 2015; Afonine et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the standard workflow in the field, supported by citations to relevant software.

claim: At near-atomic resolution, the density may not be of sufficient resolution to identify sidechain rotamers uniquely, even for bulky aromatic residues.
source: At near-atomic resolution, this manual model-building and refinement can be error prone because: (a) the density may not be of sufficient resolution to identify sidechain rotamers uniquely, even for bulky aromatic residues, making it difficult to determine sidechain-sidechain or sidechain-backbone interactions accurately
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of cryo-EM density at this resolution, based on established knowledge.

claim: For regions of non-regular secondary structure (turns or loops) or with poor local resolution, it may be difficult to position backbone atoms accurately.
source: (b) for regions of non-regular secondary structure (turns or loops) or with poor local resolution, it may be difficult to position backbone atoms accurately
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges of model building in certain regions, based on established knowledge.

claim: In regions of non-regular secondary structure or poor local resolution, precise sequence registration may be error prone.
source: (c) in these same regions, precise sequence registration may also be error prone
evidence: This is a statement about the challenges of model building in certain regions, based on established knowledge.

claim: The refinement approach proceeds in three stages.
source: Broadly, the approach proceeds in three stages.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: In the first stage, problematic residues are identified by assessing local model-strain and local agreement to density data.
source: In the first stage, we identify problematic residues by assessing local model-strain and local agreement to density data.
evidence: This is described in the methods and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Problematic regions are rebuilt against a 'training' half-map using fragment-based Monte Carlo sampling with many independent trajectories followed by all-atom refinement.
source: These problematic regions are rebuilt against a 'training' half-map using fragment-based Monte Carlo sampling with many independent trajectories followed by all-atom refinement.
evidence: This is described in the methods and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: In the second stage, the best subset of independent trajectories are selected by identifying a subset of stereochemically correct models with best agreement to an independent 'validation' half-map.
source: Second, the best subset of these independent trajectories are selected by identifying a subset of stereochemically correct models with best agreement to an independent 'validation' half-map, to prevent overfitting.
evidence: This is described in the methods and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: In the third stage, models are further optimized in the full-reconstruction with a weight optimally scaled between experimental data and the forcefield using the 'validation' half map.
source: Finally, models are further optimized in the full-reconstruction with a weight optimally scaled between experimental data and the forcefield using the 'validation' half map.
evidence: This is described in the methods and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: In incorrect regions of hand-traced models, the models fit the density well but introduce strain into nearby bond angles and torsions.
source: Moreover, when this previous approach was applied to the de novo hand-traced models from cryo-EM maps, we observed that in incorrect regions, the models still fit the density well, but did so by introducing strain into the nearby bond angles and torsions.
evidence: This observation is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Strain often occurs near the Cβ atom of aromatic residues, where strain is introduced to fit the sidechain into the density.
source: This often occurred near the Cβ atom of aromatic residues, where strain was introduced to fit the sidechain into the density (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Local strain can serve as an indicator to identify regions that could be refined to improve both the fit-to-density and the model geometry.
source: Thus, local strain can serve as an indicator to identify regions that could be refined to improve both the fit-to-density and the model geometry.
evidence: This is supported by the development and testing of the error predictor shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The new error predictor that assesses both local model-map agreement and local model-strain offers better discrimination of incorrectly versus correctly placed backbone than using density alone, with an AUPRC of 0.80 versus 0.76.
source: Using a training dataset composed of error-containing models of a cryo-EM map in which the structure has been determined by X-ray crystallography (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), we show that the new error predictor offers better discrimination of incorrectly versus correctly placed backbone, with an AUPRC (area under precision-recall curve) of 0.80 versus 0.76 using density alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from testing the error predictor, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Certain sidechains, particularly those containing negatively charged amino acids (Glu/Asp), tend to suffer from radiation damage and appear weaker in single-particle reconstructions.
source: Recent studies have shown that certain sidechains – particularly those containing negatively charged amino acids (Glu/Asp) – tend to suffer from radiation damage and thus appear weaker in single-particle reconstructions (Bartesaghi et al., 2014; Campbell et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The density of certain bulky sidechains, such as those containing Lys and Arg, tends to be less well-defined than their backbone density.
source: Moreover, the density of certain bulky sidechains, such as those containing Lys and Arg, tends to be less well-defined than their backbone density.
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of cryo-EM density, based on established knowledge and observations.

claim: Down-weighing factors for each amino acid were determined by comparing the average per-amino-acid real-space B-factor on two cryo-EM reconstructions with known high-resolution crystal structures.
source: Down-weighing factors for each amino acid were determined by comparing the average per-amino-acid real-space B-factor on two cryo-EM reconstructions with known high-resolution crystal structures (20S proteasome [Li et al., 2013] and β-galactosidase [Bartesaghi et al., 2014]), with the ratio of backbone and sidechain average B-factors being used to derive the scaling factors.
evidence: This describes the method used to derive the scaling factors, which are presented in Table 3.

claim: When the previous all-atom refinement approach was applied to very large complexes (of 800+ residues), many instances were observed in which sidechains were not properly optimized to density.
source: When our previous all-atom refinement approach was applied to very large complexes (of 800+ residues), we observed many instances in which sidechains were not properly optimized to density (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This observation is illustrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The local sidechain refinement approach resolved the sidechain fitting issue in large complexes.
source: This approach resolved this sidechain fitting issue, as shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 (right panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The magnification factor of cryo-EM may be determined with some inaccuracy, leading to errors in deciding the voxel size of the resulting single-particle reconstruction.
source: However, the magnification factor may be determined with some inaccuracy, leading to errors in deciding the voxel size of the resulting single-particle reconstruction.
evidence: This is a statement about potential sources of error in cryo-EM, based on established knowledge.

claim: Voxel size may be off by as much as several percent when using EM maps as molecular replacement targets.
source: It has been shown that voxel size may be off by as much as several percent when using EM maps as molecular replacement targets (Jackson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The voxel-size refinement strategy scales the voxel size of the map to maximize the model-map real-space correlation coefficient.
source: Here, we develop a voxel-size refinement strategy that scales the voxel size of the map to maximize the model-map real-space correlation coefficient.
evidence: This describes the method developed in this work.

claim: The iterative voxel-size refinement approach captures the general agreement between forcefield and voxel size in the presence of model errors.
source: Moreover, we investigate the robustness of our voxel-size refinement method in the presence of model errors, and demonstrate that our iterative approach captures the general agreement between forcefield and voxel size.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Following cycles of iterated voxel refinement and all-atom refinement, the voxel size shows significantly better convergence.
source: Following our iterative procedure, the deviation was much smaller, ranging from 0.99 to 1.02 (stdev = 0.004).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The refinement method is not particularly sensitive to the extent of B-factor sharpening, behaving similarly over a range of sharpening values between −40 and −130.
source: The results indicate that our refinement method is not particularly sensitive to the extent of B-factor sharpening, behaving similarly over a range of sharpening values between −40 and −130.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Independent reconstructions are used for model selection and to determine the balance between model geometry and fit-to-data during refinement.
source: In our previous approaches, we used independent reconstructions ('validation' half-map) both for model selection (DiMaio et al., 2015) and to determine the balance between model geometry and fit-to-data during refinement (DiMaio et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the approach used in this work, building on prior methods.

claim: At the final stage, several steps are performed in the context of the full reconstruction because of the additional sidechain details that may be present only in the full reconstruction.
source: At the very last stage, however, we perform several steps in the context of the full reconstruction because of the additional sidechain details that may be present only in the full reconstruction.
evidence: This describes the rationale for using the full reconstruction in the final stage.

claim: Two independent halves of the data are used to optimize the weight used with full-reconstruction data.
source: Similar to the approach adapted by the REFMAC group (Brown et al., 2015; Fernández et al., 2014), we use two independent halves of the data (the training and validation half-maps) to optimize the weight used with full-reconstruction data (see Materials and methods and (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), and that weight is used both in refinement against the full reconstruction and in voxel-size refinement.
evidence: This describes the method used, with reference to a similar approach by others.

claim: Model geometry is verified using MolProbity following refinement against the full reconstruction to ensure that it is not worsening.
source: Following refinement against the full reconstruction, model geometry is verified (using MolProbity [Chen et al., 2010]) to ensure that it is not worsening during refinement against the full reconstruction.
evidence: This describes a quality control step in the refinement protocol.

claim: EMRinger samples density around Cγ atoms as they are rotated about the χ1 dihedral angle, and identifies the angle which presents peak density for the Cγ.
source: EMRinger samples density around Cγ atoms as they are rotated about the χ1 dihedral angle, and identifies the angle which presents peak density for the Cγ.
evidence: This describes how EMRinger works, based on the cited reference.

claim: The deposited TRPV1 model (PDB id: 3J5P) was used as input to the refinement protocol.
source: The deposited model (PDB id: 3J5P) was used as input to the protocol described previously.
evidence: This describes the starting point for the TRPV1 refinement.

claim: All TRPV1 refinement was carried out using the native C4 symmetry.
source: All refinement was carried out using the native C4 symmetry.
evidence: This describes a parameter of the TRPV1 refinement.

claim: The refined TRPV1 model improves MolProbity score from 3.81 to 1.45.
source: The refined model improves model quality and maintains good model-data agreement when compared to the deposited model: the MolProbity score improves from 3.81 to 1.45
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the TRPV1 refinement, also shown in Table 1.

claim: The fit-to-data (integrated Fourier shell correlation from 10 to 3.4Å) for TRPV1 drops slightly from 0.612 to 0.607 after refinement.
source: the fit-to-data (integrated Fourier shell correlation from 10 to 3.4Å) drops slightly from 0.612 to 0.607
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the TRPV1 refinement, also shown in Table 1.

claim: The EMRinger score for TRPV1 improves from 0.65 to 2.34 after refinement.
source: but the EMRinger score improves from 0.65 to 2.34, indicating that the better fitting shown in the deposited model might result from overfitting
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the TRPV1 refinement, also shown in Table 1.

claim: The better fitting shown in the deposited TRPV1 model might result from overfitting.
source: but the EMRinger score improves from 0.65 to 2.34, indicating that the better fitting shown in the deposited model might result from overfitting
evidence: This is an inference based on the EMRinger score improvement.

claim: Closer inspection of the low-energy refined TRPV1 models identified that several made a disulfide linkage (C386–C390) that was not built in the deposited model.
source: Closer inspection of the low-energy refined models identified that serveral made a disulfide linkage (C386–C390) that was not built in the deposited model and was supported by the deposited density data (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the TRPV1 refinement, illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: The C386-C390 disulfide linkage in TRPV1 was supported by the deposited density data.
source: Closer inspection of the low-energy refined models identified that serveral made a disulfide linkage (C386–C390) that was not built in the deposited model and was supported by the deposited density data (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4B.

claim: The C386-C390 disulfide bond has previously been identified and characterized in the literature as playing an important role in the TRPV1 channel's response to oxidative stress.
source: This disulfide has previously been identified and characterized in the literature as playing an important role in the TRPV1 channel's response to oxidative stress (Chuang and Lin, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The discovery of the C386-C390 disulfide linkage illustrates the magnitude of conformational change that may be captured by the refinement protocol.
source: The discovery of this linkage also illustrates the magnitude of conformational change that may be captured by our protocol
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural changes required to form the disulfide bond.

claim: The Monte Carlo backbone sampling strategy allows refinement to overcome energy barriers that other methods using density minimization alone cannot overcome.
source: our Monte Carlo backbone sampling strategy allows refinement to overcome energy barriers that other methods using density minimization alone cannot overcome
evidence: This is an inference based on the ability to make large conformational changes.

claim: The asymmetric unit of the F420-reducing [NiFe] hydrogenase complex contains three protein chains which feature together with a [NiFe] cluster, two metal ions, four [4Fe4S] clusters that are covalently bound to cysteine sidechains, and a flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD).
source: For this, we chose the 3.4-Å reconstruction of the F420-reducing [NiFe] hydrogenase complex, in which the asymmetric unit contains three protein chains which feature together with a [NiFe] cluster, two metal ions, four [4Fe4S] clusters that are covalently bound to cysteine sidechains, and a flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) (Figure 5A).
evidence: This describes the composition of the Frh complex.

claim: The F420-reducing [NiFe] hydrogenase complex is a dodecamer with tetrahedral symmetry.
source: The complex is a dodecamer with tetrahedral symmetry, with 12 copies of a 902-residue molecule of three protein chains.
evidence: This describes the symmetry of the Frh complex.

claim: The MolProbity score for Frh improves from 3.98 to 1.59 after refinement.
source: The results of refinement are indicated in Figure 5 and Table 1; the MolProbity score improves from 3.98 to 1.59
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the Frh refinement, shown in Table 1.

claim: The EMRinger score for Frh improves from 1.06 to 2.17 after refinement.
source: and the EMRinger score improves from 1.06 to 2.17
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the Frh refinement, shown in Table 1.

claim: The iFSC for Frh drops from 0.743 to 0.708 after refinement.
source: but the iFSC drops from 0.743 to 0.708
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the Frh refinement, shown in Table 1.

claim: The decrease of fit-to-density at high-resolution shells for Frh may be a result of overfitting the deposited model to the density map.
source: We reason that the decrease of fit-to-density at high-resolution (10–3.4Å) shells may be a result of overfitting the model to the density map
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of improved geometry but decreased fit-to-density.

claim: The deposited Frh model was forced to fit the density by deviating from the likely geometry observed in high-resolution crystal structures.
source: the deposited model was forced to fit the density by deviating the likely geometry observed in high-resolution crystal structures
evidence: This is an inference based on the high number of geometry violations in the deposited model.

claim: The overfitting hypothesis for Frh is well supported by a high number of bad clashes and 39% rotamer outliers found in the deposited model.
source: This overfitting hypothesis is well supported by a high number of bad clashes and 39% rotamer outliers found in the deposited model (Table 1 and Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative data in Table 1 and Figure 5C.

claim: The deposited mitochondrial ribosome model had been previously refined with REFMAC.
source: The deposited model had been previously refined with REFMAC (Brown et al., 2015), and consists of 48 chains of proteins with 7469 amino acids assigned, and two chains of RNA with 1529 nucleic acid bases.
evidence: This describes the starting point for the mitoribosome refinement.

claim: The deposited mitochondrial ribosome model consists of 48 chains of proteins with 7469 amino acids assigned, and two chains of RNA with 1529 nucleic acid bases.
source: The deposited model had been previously refined with REFMAC (Brown et al., 2015), and consists of 48 chains of proteins with 7469 amino acids assigned, and two chains of RNA with 1529 nucleic acid bases.
evidence: This describes the composition of the mitoribosome model.

claim: For the mitoribosome, the first two stages of the protocol (fragment-based backbone rebuilding and model selection) were carried out on each protein chain individually.
source: The first two stages of the protocol (fragment-based backbone rebuilding and model selection) were carried out on each protein chain individually, whereas the third stage was carried out on the fully assembled complex.
evidence: This describes the strategy used for the mitoribosome refinement.

claim: For the mitoribosome, the third stage of refinement was carried out on the fully assembled complex.
source: The first two stages of the protocol (fragment-based backbone rebuilding and model selection) were carried out on each protein chain individually, whereas the third stage was carried out on the fully assembled complex.
evidence: This describes the strategy used for the mitoribosome refinement.

claim: Nucleic acids in the mitoribosome were not subject to geometry refinement but were included as rigid bodies throughout the whole-assembly refinement.
source: Nucleic acids were not subject to geometry refinement but were included as rigid bodies throughout the whole-assembly refinement to accurately recapitulate protein–RNA interactions.
evidence: This describes how RNA was handled in the mitoribosome refinement.

claim: Several large-scale conformational changes appear in converged mitoribosome models.
source: Several large-scale conformational changes again appear in converged models
evidence: This is a finding from the mitoribosome refinement.

claim: The refined mitoribosome models show better geometry, improved fit-to-density and fewer unexplained regions of density.
source: these models show better geometry, improved fit-to-density and fewer unexplained regions of density
evidence: This is a summary of the improvements observed in the mitoribosome refinement.

claim: The Rosetta forcefield is able to optimize hydrogen bond geometry in secondary structures without requiring prior knowledge of secondary structures.
source: In our approach, the Rosetta forcefield is able to optimize hydrogen bond geometry in secondary structures without requiring prior knowledge of secondary structures.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the Rosetta forcefield.

claim: The refined mitoribosome model has 1.50 MolProbity score, 0.676 iFSC, and 2.40 EMRinger score.
source: The refined ribosome model has 1.50 MolProbity score, 0.676 iFSC, and 2.40 EMRinger score.
evidence: These are quantitative results from the mitoribosome refinement, also shown in Table 1.

claim: The largest improvements in the mitoribosome tend to occur in regions of low local resolution (~5Å) on the periphery of the complex.
source: The largest improvements tend to occur in regions of low local resolution (~5Å assessed by ResMap [Kucukelbir et al., 2014] from the original paper) on the periphery of the complex.
evidence: This is an observation from the mitoribosome refinement results.

claim: The MolProbity score improves on all 48 protein chains of the mitoribosome.
source: Looking at the results on individual chains, the MolProbity score improves on all 48 protein chains
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and Table 1.

claim: The improvement in MolProbity score for the mitoribosome is in part because of the much-improved backbone geometry assessed by the Ramachandran favored term.
source: in part because of the much-improved backbone geometry assessed by the Ramachandran favored term in MolProbity (Figure 6A, right panel)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: EMRinger score is consistently improved for the mitoribosome, particularly in regions where the deposited model scores poorly.
source: EMRinger score is also consistently improved (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), particularly in regions where the deposited model scores poorly.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Phenix real-space refinement was carried out in the training maps for comparison with Rosetta.
source: In order to prevent refinement from fitting to noise, starting from the deposited models, we carried out phenix real-space refinement in the training maps, which contained only the half of the data used by Rosetta in the first step of the refinement procedure (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the comparison methodology.

claim: For TRPV1, phenix used 0.24 CPU hours, while Rosetta used about 5000 CPU-hours in total.
source: In the case of TRPV1, phenix used 0.24 CPU hours, generating a single model. For Rosetta, the 1000 independent trajectories take about 5 hr each, or 5000 CPU-hours in total.
evidence: This is a comparison of computational cost between the two methods.

claim: Phenix can yield models with geometry almost as good as Rosetta with much shorter run time (at most 1 hr), albeit with slightly worse density fit.
source: As shown in Table 2, with much shorter run time (at most 1 hr) phenix can yield models with geometry almost as good as Rosetta, albeit with slightly worse density fit as evaluated by both real-space correlation coefficient and iFSC.
evidence: This is a comparison of results between phenix and Rosetta, shown in Table 2.

claim: Without the Monte Carlo backbone conformational sampling used by Rosetta, models generated from phenix tend to minimally perturb the structure.
source: However, without the Monte Carlo backbone conformational sampling used by Rosetta, models generated from phenix tend to minimally perturb the structure, and cannot provide the large backbone corrections shown by our new approach.
evidence: This is a comparison of the capabilities of the two methods.

claim: Models generated from phenix cannot provide the large backbone corrections shown by the Rosetta approach.
source: However, without the Monte Carlo backbone conformational sampling used by Rosetta, models generated from phenix tend to minimally perturb the structure, and cannot provide the large backbone corrections shown by our new approach.
evidence: This is a comparison of the capabilities of the two methods.

claim: The method can improve model geometry significantly while maintaining good agreement to the density data in all three test systems.
source: In all cases, we show that we are able to improve model geometry significantly while maintaining good agreement to the density data.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings, supported by the data in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Model convergence can be used to suggest local model uncertainty in addition to B-factors.
source: We show that model convergence can be used to suggest local model uncertainty in addition to B-factors.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A for TRPV1.

claim: The refined models recover structure features that are supported in the literature or that are in much better local agreement with the density data.
source: Finally, we also show that our models also recover structure features that are supported in the literature, or that are in much better local agreement with the density data.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the C386-C390 disulfide bond in TRPV1 and the improved β-sheet geometry in mitoribosome chain k.

claim: The approach can automatically perform large-scale backbone reorganization, correcting backbone placement errors common in 3–4.5Å resolution datasets.
source: Unlike other approaches (Brown et al., 2015; Headd et al., 2012), our approach can automatically perform large-scale backbone reorganization, correcting backbone placement errors common in these 3–4.5Å resolution datasets.
evidence: This is a key distinguishing feature of the method, demonstrated in the results.

claim: The use of a physically realistic forcefield throughout refinement handles the under-constrained nature of refinement at 3-4.5Å resolutions.
source: First, the use a physically realistic forcefield throughout refinement handles the under-constrained nature of refinement at these resolutions, using chemical 'domain knowledge' learned from high-resolution crystal structures to implicitly fill in the missing information in the data.
evidence: This is a statement about the role of the forcefield in the method.

claim: Fragment-based rebuilding explicitly samples the most likely backbone conformations given a short stretch of sequence, using prior information gathered from high-resolution protein structures.
source: Second, our fragment-based rebuilding , which explicitly samples the most likely backbone conformations given a short stretch of sequence, also uses prior information gathered from high-resolution protein structures, further restricting conformation space and filling in additional information that is not present in the data.
evidence: This is a statement about how fragment-based rebuilding works.

claim: In all cases, the high-resolution density-fit (evaluated by FSC integrated from 10–3.4Å resolution shells) drops slightly after Rosetta structure refinement.
